summary: Summarizes experience with the Jabber scribe role at IETF meetings, in which volunteers relay discussion between the meeting room and a text chat room, and offers suggestions for doing it well. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: At a meeting, a helper types what is said into a chat so people who are not in the room can follow. This gives tips for doing that job.

questions: what does a jabber scribe do at ietf meetings
how do remote participants engage at ietf
subtitle: Volunteers who relay meeting discussions to online participants

tldr.problem: Remote participants at IETF meetings cannot fully engage because they are listening to audio or watching video while being unable to provide real-time feedback to the physical room.
tldr.mechanism: Jabber scribes sit in the meeting room and use text chatrooms to relay questions and comments from remote participants to the discussion, and relay speaker names and key information back to the chatroom.
tldr.outcome: Remote participants can participate and provide feedback almost in real time, making IETF meetings more inclusive. The role is now historic as other technologies have become available.

today: RFC 7649 is a Historic document. It describes practices that were common for IETF meetings, but other technologies have since become available for remote participation.

sections.title: The Jabber Scribe Role
sections.content:
During IETF meetings, volunteers help sessions run smoothly by serving as a bridge between the physical meeting room and an online text chatroom. These volunteers, called Jabber scribes, relay information back and forth using Jabber/XMPP messaging technology. The role is important because it allows remote participants, who are listening to the audio stream or watching a video stream, to provide real-time feedback and comments into the meeting.

RFC 7649 summarizes experience with the Jabber scribe role and provides practical suggestions for fulfilling it effectively. The document explains that while the scribe role appears to require complete transcription of discussions, most volunteers are not expected to do that. Instead, they perform three key tasks: relaying questions and comments from remote participants to the physical room, counting or tallying responses from chatroom participants (such as votes or hums), and providing relevant information from the room back to the chatroom.
sections.plainLanguage: A Jabber scribe is a helper who types what is happening in a meeting into a chat room so people on a video call can follow along and send questions back.

sections.title: Who the Scribe Serves
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three kinds of chatroom participants, each with different needs. Remote participants are listening to the audio stream or watching a video feed and want to send questions back to the room. Observers are IETF attendees in other physical rooms watching the chatroom to know when to come to this session or to see what is being discussed. Local participants are in the same physical room and sometimes follow the chatroom to track the discussion.

Remote participants are the primary customers for the scribe. The scribe may ask in the chatroom to determine if there are indeed remote participants present, as it can happen that all chatroom participants are local and do not require intensive service from a scribe.
sections.plainLanguage: The scribe helps remote people on the call, people watching from other rooms, and sometimes the people in the room itself. The remote people are the most important audience.

sections.title: Core Responsibilities
sections.content:
The primary tasks of a Jabber scribe are to relay questions and comments from the chatroom to the physical room by going to the microphone and speaking them aloud, and to relay information from the room back to the chatroom. In particular, scribes count or tally chatroom participants who virtually 'hum' or vote on questions, and relay that count to the physical room. They also relay the tallies of hums and votes from the physical room back to the chatroom after asking the session chairs for a readout.

Additional tasks that experienced scribes often undertake include relaying the names of speakers to the chatroom (so remote participants know who is speaking), relaying slide numbers or titles, providing links to relevant documents, and relaying logistical or technical information about the meeting or audio stream quality. Scribes may relay the gist of ad hoc discussions when slides are not available, though complete transcription is not expected unless arranged in advance with the session chairs.
sections.plainLanguage: The main job is to read questions from the chat to the room and tell the chat what is happening. Scribes also count votes and share links to help remote people follow along.

sections.title: Getting Set Up and Staying Effective
sections.content:
Before a session begins, the scribe should coordinate with session chairs to ensure remote participants have information about where to find materials, the agenda, and the audio stream. The scribe should also join the chatroom well in advance using a Jabber/XMPP client and open browser windows with the session agenda, overall IETF meeting agenda, session materials page, and remote participation page.

During the session, the scribe should identify themselves to both the physical room and the chatroom, and ask chatroom participants what level of information they need relayed. A common practice is to ask participants to prepend statements they want relayed with 'RELAY' or 'MIC' to make them easier to identify. When relaying, the scribe should say 'this is X relaying for Y from the chatroom' so people know the scribe is not speaking for themselves. The RFC notes that a lag of 20 seconds to 2 minutes exists between the physical room and the audio stream, plus the time for a remote participant to type a question, which is why scribes are often given privilege to go to the front of the microphone line.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the meeting, talk to the organizers and open some web pages. During the meeting, tell people you are the scribe, and when you read a question, say who it is from so everyone knows you are relaying.

sections.title: Managing Problems and Responsibilities
sections.content:
When chatroom participants become abusive or inappropriate, the scribe is not obligated to relay such comments verbatim. Instead, a suitable approach is to ask the contributor to rephrase in a more constructive way. However, the scribe is not responsible for managing poor behavior in the session; that responsibility lies with the session chairs.

The RFC notes that because IETF chatrooms are not locked down with nickname registration requirements, social-engineering attacks and denial-of-service attacks (such as flooding the chatroom with unwanted traffic) are possible. A scribe should be aware of this possibility. Additionally, when chatroom participants speak anonymously or use only a nickname, the scribe should ask for clarification so that the identity can be communicated at the microphone, in accordance with the IETF 'Note Well' that applies to chatroom contributions as well as in-room statements.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone says something rude in chat, you can ask them to say it more nicely. The organizers are responsible for keeping order, not the scribe. Be careful because some people might try to cause trouble.
